title: PSA: if all your edge weights are 1, you do not need Dijkstra
author: heap_of_trouble
body:
Reviewed a bunch of solutions this week and this keeps coming up, so:

**Unweighted graph, shortest path? BFS.** Plain, boring BFS with a deque. It is O(V + E) and it is correct, because BFS visits vertices in nondecreasing distance order by construction.

Dijkstra on the same graph is O((V + E) log V), needs a priority queue, and gives you the identical answer. You paid a log factor and a heap allocation for nothing.

The one in between that people miss: **weights of only 0 and 1 -> 0-1 BFS.** Use a deque, push-front on a 0 edge, push-back on a 1 edge. Still linear.

```python
dq = deque([start])
dist[start] = 0
while dq:
    u = dq.popleft()
    for v, w in adj[u]:
        if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
            dist[v] = dist[u] + w
            dq.appendleft(v) if w == 0 else dq.append(v)
```

Rough rule I use: unweighted -> BFS. Weights in {0,1} -> 0-1 BFS. Small integer weights -> consider bucket queue. Arbitrary non-negative -> Dijkstra. Negative edges -> Bellman-Ford and go sit down and think about what you have done.

replies.author: tail_recursive
replies.body:
The negative-edge line is funny but it's worth spelling out *why* Dijkstra breaks, because "it just doesn't work" isn't an explanation.

Dijkstra finalises a vertex the moment it pops it, on the assumption that no shorter path can turn up later. That assumption is exactly "adding an edge never decreases the total". A negative edge violates it, so you can pop a vertex, mark it done, and then discover a shorter route to it that you'll now ignore.

replies.author: off_by_one
replies.body:
small correction to the snippet: that conditional-expression-as-statement form works but linters hate it and it reads badly. plain if/else is clearer here.

also if you're doing 0-1 BFS you want the `dist[u] + w < dist[v]` check rather than a visited set, since a vertex can legitimately be improved after first being reached.
